response.query: Which detector evaluation metrics and reporting standards (sensitivity, specificity, language stratification) minimize false-positive harms across disciplines?
response.answer: Sensitivity and specificity minimize false-positive harms by ensuring true positives and correctly identifying negatives. High specificity reduces false positives, crucial in contexts where incorrect positives are costly. Balancing sensitivity and specificity is key to effective diagnostic testing.

results.title: What is Sensitivity, Specificity, False positive, False negative?
results.content: # What is Sensitivity, Specificity, False positive, False negative? When using known samples of a disease, sensitivity and specificity variables can be calculated for evaluation of the test and its results. * Sensitivity and specificity are independent of the population of interest subject to the tests while Positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) is used when considering the value of a test to a clinician and are dependent on the prevalence of the disease in the population of interest. * The **positive predictive value (PPV)** is the probability that a subject/sample that returns a positive result really is positive and the **negative predictive value (NPV)** is the probability that a subject/sample that returns a negative result really is negative. * Sensitivity is the ability of a test to correctly identify those patients with the disease.

results.title: Difference between Sensitivity and Specificity - GeeksforGeeks
results.content: Sensitivity measures the model's ability to correctly identify actual positive cases. It ensures that important instances of interest are not missed whereas specificity focuses on correctly identifying actual negative cases and minimising false alarms by ensuring that non-problematic cases are not mistakenly flagged. Sensitivity is also termed as Recall or True Positive Rate which measures how well true positives are identified by a test or model. \text{Sensitivity} = \frac{\text{True Positives}}{\text{True Positives} + \text{False Negatives}}. Specificity is also termed as True Negative Rate which measures how well the model correctly identifies negative cases i.e the ones that should not trigger a positive prediction. In simpler words specificity depicts among all the negative cases how many were correctly identified as negative by the model. \text{Specificity} = \frac{\text{True Negatives}}{\text{True Negatives} + \text{False Positives}}. High specificity means few false positives. In binary classification tasks choosing between sensitivity and specificity depends on the relative cost of false positives versus false negatives in the specific application domain. Specificity is important when your goal is to minimize false positives especially in environments where flagging a negative instance incorrectly leads to high costs, waste or user dissatisfaction. > Sensitivity ensures that the true positives aren't missed whereas specificity ensures that false positives are labelled correctly. A model which has a high sensitivity but low specificity would catch all the positive cases but flood the system with false alarms. Similarly a model with low sensitivity and high specificity may miss critical cases therefore it is important to achieve the right balance between sensitivity and specificity. + Introduction to Machine Learning8 min read. + Types of Machine Learning7 min read. + Applications of Machine Learning3 min read. + Machine Learning with Python Tutorial5 min read. + Supervised Machine Learning7 min read. + Linear Regression in Machine learning14 min read. + Logistic Regression in Machine Learning10 min read. + Decision Tree in Machine Learning8 min read. + Random Forest Algorithm in Machine Learning5 min read. + Hierarchical Clustering in Machine Learning6 min read. + Evaluation Metrics in Machine Learning9 min read. + Regularization in Machine Learning5 min read. + Cross Validation in Machine Learning5 min read. + Bias and Variance in Machine Learning6 min read.

results.title: Sensitivity and Specificity Explained
results.content: Two key statistical measures—**sensitivity** and **specificity**—are fundamental in understanding how well a diagnostic test performs. Sensitivity is the ability of a test to correctly identify those patients who have the disease (true positives). Specificity, on the other hand, measures the ability of a test to correctly identify individuals who do not have the disease (true negatives). A highly specific test will have few false positives, ensuring that healthy individuals are not incorrectly identified as having the disease. Both sensitivity and specificity are crucial for evaluating diagnostic tests. The formulas used for sensitivity and specificity rely on the classification of test outcomes. Interpreting sensitivity and specificity correctly is essential for understanding the performance of diagnostic tests. For instance, screening tests for serious conditions like HIV or cancer often prioritize sensitivity to minimize the chances of a false negative, while confirmatory tests prioritize specificity 4 to avoid misdiagnosis. No diagnostic test can achieve 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity simultaneously. The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve is a graphical representation that displays the trade-offs between sensitivity (true positive rate) and \(1 - \text{specificity}\) (false positive rate) at various threshold settings. The decision threshold in diagnostic testing determines when a test outcome is considered positive or negative. Even though sensitivity and specificity are extensively used to evaluate diagnostic tests, there are pitfalls that can impact their validity and interpretation. + **High Specificity, Low Sensitivity:** A test might appear exceptionally accurate because it correctly identifies most negatives but fails to catch rare positives. The principles of sensitivity and specificity form the backbone of diagnostic test evaluation in modern medicine. * **Sensitivity** measures the ability of a test to correctly identify those with a disease, while **specificity** measures its ability to correctly identify those without it. * Interpreting sensitivity and specificity involves understanding true positives, false negatives, false positives, and true negatives. * Diagnostic tests often involve a trade-off between sensitivity and specificity, which can be visually represented via ROC curves. In summary, sensitivity and specificity are not merely abstract statistical concepts but are real-world tools that directly influence the accuracy and success of diagnostic testing.
